articles.title: Tings Chak: How Brazil’s election could reshape relations with China - Friends of Socialist China
articles.summary: Tings Chak: How Brazil’s election could reshape relations with China  Friends of Socialist China
articles.full_text:
The following article by Tings Chak, Asia Co-Coordinator of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and an editor of the international edition of Wenhua Zongheng: A Journal of Contemporary Chinese Thought, examines what is at stake for China-Brazil relations in Brazil’s presidential runoff on October 25 between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro.
Over the past two decades, Brazil and China have built a political partnership that “has expanded the space for independent action among countries of the Global South”. Under Lula, this cooperation has extended to industrial development, infrastructure, science and technology – and to Brazil’s popular movements, with the Landless Workers’ Movement (MST) working with Chinese institutions on agricultural mechanisation, bioinputs and AI tools for agroecology built on Chinese open-source models.
Flávio Bolsonaro, by contrast, has offered Brazil to Washington as the “solution” to its dependence on China for critical minerals, and his campaign has proposed preventing Brazil’s Pix payment system from connecting to non-Western networks. With the Trump administration proclaiming a “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, Brazil – Latin America’s largest economy and a founding member of BRICS – has become “a consequential battleground in Washington’s campaign to contain China’s growing relations with the region”.
Tings notes that Chinese analysts anticipate “cold politics, hot economics” under a Flávio presidency, with commodity trade continuing but strategic cooperation deteriorating, as it did under his father. She concludes that the future of China-Brazil cooperation “will depend on the capacity of organised popular forces to build a sovereign national project and turn international cooperation into lasting changes in people’s lives”.
This article first appeared in BreakThrough News.
On October 25, Brazilians will return to the polls to choose between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for his role in an attempted coup. The first round gave Flávio 47% of valid votes against Lula’s 45%, revealing the enduring strength of the far right four years after its electoral defeat. The runoff takes place as Donald Trump seeks to restore US domination over Latin America, with Brazil emerging as a consequential battleground in Washington’s campaign to contain China’s growing relations with the region.
Over the past two decades, Brazil and China have built a political partnership that has expanded the space for independent action among countries of the Global South. Under Lula and Xi Jinping, this relationship has deepened through cooperation in industrial development, infrastructure, science, and technology. The election will determine whether this project advances or Brazil’s international orientation is subordinated to Washington’s renewed Monroe Doctrine as part of the continent’s rightward shift.
Since Lula’s return to the presidency in 2023, the two governments have connected Chinese cooperation with Brazil’s development programs, including Nova Indústria Brasil, the Growth Acceleration Program (PAC), and the Ecological Transformation Plan. Lula’s May 2025 visit to Beijing produced 36 agreements covering infrastructure, finance, artificial intelligence, public health, and industrial cooperation. Behind these agreements is a long-standing challenge: overcoming Brazil’s dependent position in the international division of labor, where commodity exports continue to outweigh advanced industrial and technological development.
This cooperation has also reached Brazilian popular movements. Through the International Association for Popular Cooperation (Baobab), Brazil’s Landless Rural Workers’ Movement (MST) and other organizations have worked with Chinese institutions on agricultural mechanization, bioinputs, and digital technologies for family farming. These initiatives include the Digital Family Farming and Agroecology Laboratory and IARAA, an artificial intelligence project for agroecology and agrarian reform developed by Brazilian popular movements using Chinese open-source models. In a countryside marked by extreme concentrations of land, machinery, and capital, such cooperation offers new tools to peasant organizations fighting for agrarian reform and the production of healthy food.
Brazil’s relationship with China also reveals the different class interests at work in the country, with contradictions particularly visible in the countryside. Massive exports of soybeans, meat, and minerals have continued under both Bolsonaro and Lula, but their governments have pursued very different political relationships with Beijing. While Jair Bolsonaro attacked China and aligned himself with Washington, Lula has sought to deepen strategic cooperation, including in industrial development, technology, and agrarian reform. Flávio Bolsonaro now promises an “economically pragmatic” relationship with China while cultivating close ties with Trump. For sectors of Brazil’s ruling classes that profit from commodity exports, continuing to sell to China while embracing Washington’s political agenda presents little contradiction. For Brazil’s efforts to rebuild its industry and develop technological sovereignty, the consequences are far greater.
The return of the Monroe Doctrine
Washington’s ambitions were made explicit in its November 2025 National Security Strategy, which announced a “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, seeking to restore US pre-eminence in the Western Hemisphere and deny outside powers control over strategic resources and infrastructure. Five days later, China published its third Latin America policy paper, reaffirming sovereignty, non-interference, regional integration, technological cooperation, and support for the region as a Zone of Peace. The two documents reveal fundamentally different approaches to the political future of the continent.
Brazil’s position is decisive. As Latin America’s largest economy, a founding BRICS member, and a leading participant in Mercosur, it possesses industrial, scientific, and political capacities that could strengthen independent development across Latin America and beyond.
The emergence of a new technological era makes this struggle particularly consequential. Brazil is among the few countries of the Global South capable of pursuing digital and technological sovereignty that could benefit its neighbors and parts of Africa. Its roughly 23% share of global rare earth reserves is an important starting point, but control over minerals alone is insufficient. The greater challenge is developing the capacity to process them, manufacture advanced components, and build the digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence systems, and technologies that will shape future production.
Flávio has made his orientation clear. Speaking at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in the United States in March 2026, he offered Brazil as the “solution” to Washington’s dependence on China for critical minerals, explicitly linking rare earths to artificial intelligence and US military superiority. Chinese economic reporting has also described proposals from his team to exclude China from rare-earth supply chains. Rather than using Brazil’s resources to develop its own industrial and technological capacities, this agenda would place them at the service of US technological and military power.
The same political orientation extends to digital sovereignty. In July 2026, Flávio’s campaign submitted proposals to US trade authorities that included preventing Brazil’s Pix payment system from connecting to non-Western international payment networks and loosening commitments within Mercosur. These proposals converge with a wider US campaign involving tariffs, digital regulation, strategic minerals, and attempts to influence Brazil’s electoral process. Meanwhile, Washington’s January 2026 bombing on Venezuela and kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro and Cilia Flores demonstrated how far it is prepared to go to impose its will on the continent.
BRICS and the struggle for an independent foreign policy
Brazil, particularly under Lula, has helped build institutions through which countries of the Global South can reduce their dependence on Western-dominated structures. At the July 2025 BRICS summit in Rio de Janeiro, the group advanced cooperation on development finance, local-currency transactions, and international institutional reform. The New Development Bank, headed by former Brazilian president Dilma Rousseff, is an important expression of this effort.
The BRICS cannot automatically overcome economic dependency or guarantee sovereignty for working people. Yet its expansion offers greater room for independent development, provided that participating governments have the political commitment to use these possibilities.
Brazil’s history reveals how difficult that independence has been to defend. In 1961, vice-president João Goulart became the first high-ranking representative of a Latin American government to visit the People’s Republic of China, meeting Mao Zedong when revolutionary China remained diplomatically isolated and subjected to US sanctions. Three years later, Goulart was overthrown in a US-backed civil-military coup that inaugurated a 21-year dictatorship. The early history of China–Brazil friendship was inseparable from struggles over national sovereignty, agrarian reform, and the forces determined to suppress them.
The international material conditions for South–South cooperation are considerably more favorable today, but political direction remains decisive. Jair Bolsonaro hosted the 2019 BRICS summit in Brasília while pursuing close alignment with Washington. A government can weaken institutions from within by abandoning the commitments that give them political substance.
The far right’s resurgence also reflects the enduring power of Brazil’s own ruling classes. B

articles.title: Lula or Bolsonaro: Why Brazil's presidential election matters for Brics and India - The Times of India
articles.summary: Lula or Bolsonaro: Why Brazil's presidential election matters for Brics and India  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
When 
Brics
 leaders met in New Delhi last month, Brazil’s President Lula da Silva was conspicuously absent from the Bharat Mandapam. He was campaigning for the crucial fourth term back home, so his foreign minister Mauro Vieira arrived in the capital for the "non-West" summit.
That absence could now highlight the Brics' road ahead, at least for the time US President Donald Trump occupies the White House.
Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. This is what Brics stood for when India hosted it on September 12. However, the real B of Brics, which is Brazil, has the world's attention.
(From left) Egyptian president Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Russian president Vladimir Putin, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chinese president Xi Jinping and South African president Cyril Ramaphosa during a joint tree plantation initiative during the 18th Brics Summit, at the Bharat Mandapam, in New Delhi.
On 25 October, Brazilians will choose between Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, and the winner will decide how deeply one of the bloc’s founding members keeps investing in it.
Flávio Bolsonaro leads the race into the runoff (second round of voting) after securing 47 per cent of the first-round vote, against Lula’s 45 per cent. Brazil mandates a second round of voting if no candidate secures a majority (more than 50 per cent) in the first round. Therefore, for a grouping already stretched by its own expansion, the result matters well beyond South America.
Results after first round of voting in Brazil.
A bloc pulled in three directions
Brics began with five members and grew to eleven after the 2024 expansion, with Indonesia the newest, joining in 2025. 
Brazil opposed the enlargement, particularly because of the one nation. Iran. It feared that adding the avowedly anti-West Islamic Republic would cost the group its cohesion. Like India, Brazil wants Brics to be reformist and not revolutionary, thereby limiting it to a body that argues for change inside the existing order rather than one that tries to replace it.
Vieira, putting the Brazilian view plainly in the run-up to the 2026 summit, said that “a multipolar world that promises peace and prosperity must not be confused with a world of spheres of influence.” In other words, Brasília wants rules that bind the strong as well as the weak.
Brazil had some success as the New Delhi declaration reaffirmed support for the United Nations system and the Paris climate agreement, going further than the G7, whose latest declarations did not mention the climate pact.
However, these are words and not actions, and Russia, a Brics member, has ignored the UN Charter in recent years. Even so, agreeing to acknowledge the UN’s legitimacy was a better outcome than blocking any mention of it.
Brics continues to expand unlike the West-dominated G7.
Those gains on paper may not last, as Brazil’s place in the bloc will depend largely on its next president. The world’s two biggest powers have very different visions for what Brics should become. Both Washington and Beijing are seeking to tilt the balance in their favour.
The United States, under Donald Trump, has made clear what it wants from Brazil. The Trump administration imposed heavy trade duties on Brazilian exports in July 2025, in retaliation for what it called a judicial “witch hunt” against former President Jair Bolsonaro, who Trump see as his "ally".
It has sanctioned the Supreme Court justice who prosecuted him and revoked the visas of several justices. It also accepted Flávio Bolsonaro’s appeal in May to designate two Brazilian criminal groups as foreign terrorist organisations, while Lula’s alternative proposals went unanswered.
Beyond one man’s fate
A Bolsonaro win would help realign Latin America behind an America First agenda of militarised approaches to crime, crackdowns on migration and preferential access to critical minerals and energy. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves, and Washington wants to reduce its dependence on China for them.
On the trade and commerce front, Bolsonaro has criticised non-dollar initiatives, which is exactly the kind of de-dollarisation talk that makes some Brics ideas unwelcome in Washington. His platform does not mention Brics at all, and he has entertained the idea of leaving the group.
Beijing sits on the other side of the ledger, and its leverage is economic. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009. It buys nearly 30 per cent of Brazil’s total exports, including soybeans, crude oil and iron ore, and it has become a major investor in electricity, mining, cars and oil.
The Brics has outperformed G7 over the last two decades.
A Brics that China hopes to make firmer and more assertive is difficult to build without Brazil, the largest economy in Latin America. That is why a Brazilian drift towards Washington would be felt in Beijing, even if it never became a formal exit.
Nevertheless, the challenge with China is intricate, as even under Jair Bolsonaro, anti-Beijing rhetoric did not stop bilateral trade from reaching record levels, and Brazil resisted US pressure to exclude Huawei from its 5G rollout. Flávio Bolsonaro’s own programme envisages continued commercial engagement with China. A withdrawal from Brics, in short, is possible but far from inevitable.
Therefore, a Bolsonaro government could stay inside the main multilateral bodies while withdrawing from the effort to give them energy, shifting from coalition-building among middle powers to a transactional, bilateral relationship with Washington.
Lula, by contrast, has pursued what officials call “multi-alignment”, keeping a working relationship with the United States, expanding trade with China and using Brics, the G20 and UN climate talks to widen Brazil’s room for manoeuvre.
Brics constitutes 40% of the global GDP.
A state under strain
The foreign policy debate is real, but it is not what most Brazilians say drives their vote. Crime is a central worry, and Bolsonaro’s “mano dura”, or iron fist, approach appeals to voters tired of violence in their neighbourhoods.
Education is another concern, as a recent poll found that 71 per cent of Brazilians are weighing it in their vote, and 83 per cent believe it should be among the next government’s top three priorities.
Only 66 per cent of Grade 2 children met basic literacy requirements in 2025, well short of the 80 per cent target for 2030.
On the US relationship, voters appear to lean towards Lula. Polls show his popularity rose after his frequent disagreements with Trump over trade and security, and other surveys found Brazilians blamed Bolsonaro more for the tariffs imposed in July.
A woman at a voting centre in US to participate in Brazil's general election. (Reuters photo)
The Brazilian Association of Institutional and Governmental Relations says the same pressure would follow Bolsonaro into office.
Its president, Jean Castro, said: “He cannot adopt a stance that could be mistaken for subservience.”
Behind these campaign themes lies a harder question. Can Brazil actually deliver on what it promises abroad? Brasilia's influence depends on partners believing that today’s deals will survive tomorrow’s politics, and that this belief is eroding.
More than 90 per cent of the federal government’s non-interest spending is mandatory, leaving little room for infrastructure, which Brazil needs if it is to make use of its mineral reserves.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects that government debt will reach about 98 per cent of GDP by the end of 2026. Real interest rates sit near 10 per cent, so servicing that debt consumes funds that could strengthen security forces or support strategic goals.
Adding to that, criminal networks operate across more than 1,500 clandestine airstrips in the Amazon basin and move drugs, gold and weapons across borders with Brazil’s ten neighbours.
Responsibility for fighting them is split among federal police, highway police, an intelligence agency, police forces in 26 states and the federal district, the armed forces and prosecutors. Efforts to bring them under one authority have failed in Congress. The result is that decisions about gangs operating from Brazilian soil are increasingly taken elsewhere, as Washington’s terrorist designations show.
The third problem is trust in the courts because since late 2025, the public has learned how far parts of the judiciary became entangled with the Banco Master affair.
The bank’s owner is alleged to have made side payments and awarded lucrative contracts to families of Supreme Court justices, and to have lent his private jets to justices.
Flavio Bolsonaro is himself under investigation over alleged links to the bank, and figures close to Lula’s government have also been drawn in.
The winner will appoint at least three of the court’s 11 justices, reshaping the institution that is meant to hold the next government to account.
The neighbourhood also offers little relief. Brazil once led the creation of regional institutions such as Mercosur, but it is now increasingly isolated in South America. Its relationship with Argentina, which helped underpin four decades of regional stability, has deteriorated to the point that neither country has an ambassador in the other’s capital.
Where India stands
India could probably be the member with the most to lose from a Brics that becomes either a Chinese-led counterweight to the West or an empty shell.
India has a significant interest in Brazil's political direction, given its economic ties with the Latin American nation. Bilateral trade exceeded $15 billion in 2025, making Brazil India's biggest trading partner in Latin America. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva have set a target of taking bilateral trade to $20 billion by 2030.

articles.title: "Annual limit of 350,000 units" China concedes hybrid vehicle exports under EU trade pressure, but prospects for securing alternative markets and local production appear challenging - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: "Annual limit of 350,000 units" China concedes hybrid vehicle exports under EU trade pressure, but prospects for securing alternative markets and local production appear challenging  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
Discussion expected on China trade imbalance and industry damage response at EU summit
China maintains optimism despite hybrid vehicle export limits, but market skepticism persists
Expansion of local production by Chinese automakers in Europe faces burdens from production costs and local procurement regulations
There are forecasts that trade relations with China will emerge as a key agenda at the European Union (EU) summit. As trade imbalances deepen and conflicts between the two sides intensify, international attention is focused on the EU’s further response measures. Recently, China has made some concessions, such as agreeing to limit hybrid vehicle export volumes amid tense trade relations, but considering sluggish domestic demand and high entry barriers in alternative export markets, it appears difficult to reduce dependence on Europe in the short term.
EU struggles with trade deficit against China
According to Reuters on the 14th (local time), leaders of the 27 EU member states will hold a summit on the 15th-16th in Brussels, Belgium, to discuss damage to regional industries and trade response measures caused by a surge in imports of Chinese automobiles and manufactured goods. The EU's trade deficit in goods with China reached 360 billion euros (about US$419 billion) last year, and hit 200 billion euros (about US$233 billion) in the first half of this year. This deficit is occurring not only in automobiles, which have been the main source of conflict between the two sides, but also across manufactured goods including machinery, textiles, basic metals, and chemicals, raising growing concerns over weakening competitiveness and employment declines among regional companies.
Meanwhile, the policy direction of the EU Commission is shifting toward curbing the influx of Chinese products into the region. A representative example is the imposition of high tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Since 2023, the Commission has conducted an anti-subsidy investigation on Chinese EVs for about a year, and in July 2024, it imposed provisional countervailing duties on Chinese EVs, judging that Chinese government subsidies distorted competition in the regional market. This was the first large-scale trade sanction against Chinese EVs. In October of the same year, the EU finalized, with member states' approval, additional tariffs up to 35.3% on Chinese EVs per company. These tariffs are added to the existing 10% tariff on vehicle imports and will be applied from October 30, 2024, for five years.
China limits hybrid vehicle import volumes
Amid this trade pressure, China recently made some concessions in negotiations with the EU, easing tensions. On the 12th, the Financial Times reported that the Commission is pushing a plan to limit annual import volumes of Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to 350,000 units. This agreement was reached during trade talks between Maroš Šefčovič, EU Commissioner for Trade, and Wang Wentao, China's Minister of Commerce, held in Beijing on the 8th-9th. The import limit will be implemented in December this year, setting an annual import cap at 350,000 units in 2027, with a 6% annual increase starting in 2028, through 2030.
The restriction applies to hybrid vehicles produced in China and exported to the EU, including vehicles manufactured by European automakers in their Chinese plants. However, vehicles of Chinese brands produced within the EU are exempt from the import quota. The EU estimates China's hybrid vehicle exports to the EU will reach about 800,000 units this year. This agreement aims to reduce the import volume of Chinese hybrid vehicles by more than half and lower their market share from the current approximately 6% to around 3% within the regional market.
"Exports will rather expand," China's confidence
On the other hand, China claims that this agreement creates opportunities for expanding exports of its enterprises. On the 12th, China's Ministry of Commerce released an official statement noting, "According to EU statistics, EU imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles were 107,000 units in 2024 and rose to 302,000 units in 2025," adding that "both sides agreed to expand imports based on 2025 volumes, ensuring export capacity and stable growth for Chinese companies." While the EU emphasizes the reduction effect based on expected imports this year, China highlights that the agreement allows increasing export volumes based on last year's actual import figure of 302,000 units.
Additionally, China’s Ministry of Commerce explained that the hybrid vehicle trade agreement is based on three principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination, and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. Regarding the non-discrimination principle, it stated, "No measures should target only Chinese products or discriminate against Chinese companies," and added, "The import quota allocated to China will not be less than that allocated to any other import source country in the EU." On WTO compliance, it affirmed, "China retains all rights within the WTO framework, including initiating dispute settlement procedures and requesting trade remedies."
Table 1. Chinese Hybrid Vehicle Import Restriction Plan and Positions of Both Sides
| Category | Main content | 
|---|---|
| Import Restriction Plan | Set an annual import limit of 350,000 Chinese hybrid vehicles in 2027, with a 6% annual increase from 2028 through 2030 | 
| EU Position | Measure to reduce Chinese hybrid vehicle inflow by more than half compared to this year's expected imports and lower market share | 
| China's Position | Quota increases compared to last year's actual imports, making the agreement favorable for export expansion and stable growth | 
Difficulty in seeking alternative markets
However, skepticism remains about China's optimism in the market. There are concerns that China will face difficulties absorbing its existing European export volumes in other markets. First, the Chinese domestic automobile market is sluggish due to weakened consumer sentiment and reduced purchase subsidies. According to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), domestic passenger car sales in China were about 1.63 million units in September, a 28.1% year-on-year decline, marking the 12th consecutive month of decrease. Entry barriers in alternative export markets are also rising. The U.S. has imposed a 100% additional tariff on Chinese EVs and tightened regulations on Chinese connected car software and hardware, effectively blocking market entry. Mexico approved a bill last December imposing tariffs up to 50% on about 1,400 items, including automobiles imported from non-FTA countries such as China, while Brazil raised tariffs on imported electric and hybrid vehicles to 35% starting July.
Absorption capacity in existing major export markets is also limited. According to a March report by global accounting firm PwC, Chinese exports of passenger and light commercial vehicles to Russia fell sharply by 46% to about 556,000 units last year due to factors such as increased import taxes by the Russian government and weakening domestic vehicle demand. Southeast Asia, targeted by China as a new export hub, is relatively small in scale. PwC data shows that automobile sales in six major ASEAN countries—Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Philippines, Vietnam, and Singapore—totaled about 3.5 million units last year, with Chinese automakers holding only 11% market share.
Uncertain effectiveness of local production strategies
Under these circumstances, Chinese companies are striving to establish local production and supply chains in Europe to open new paths. On the 12th, Stella Li, BYD’s Senior Vice Chairman, told French economic broadcaster BFM Business in an interview that the company plans to secure two additional production hubs in Europe, with France being a strong candidate. BYD already built its first complete car production plant in Europe in Hungary, which is scheduled to begin full operation in the fourth quarter this year. Additionally, XPeng continues contract manufacturing through Magna International’s factory in Austria and is considering partnering with local manufacturers to build new factories or utilize existing ones. Changan Automobile also aims to expand its European production capacity to 180,000 units annually by 2028 and 350,000 units by 2030.
The problem is that expanding local production in Europe may not directly enhance the competitiveness of Chinese companies. They have to bear higher labor and energy costs in Europe compared to China and incur additional expenses while establishing new local parts supply chains. Furthermore, the direction of the EU’s industrial regulations remains unsettled. The Commission is currently promoting stricter local production and parts procurement requirements for EVs under the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), with ongoing debates among member states and industries over the scope of products recognized as European. Controversies persist over whether vehicles and parts produced in non-EU countries such as Turkey, the UK, and Morocco should be recognized as European. Chinese automakers risk additional burdens of adjusting their parts procurement and production systems depending on the regulations finalized in the future.

articles.title: China Returns to U.S. Soybeans With Major Purchases After Trump-Xi Summit - AgroLatam
articles.summary: China Returns to U.S. Soybeans With Major Purchases After Trump-Xi Summit  AgroLatam
articles.full_text:
Chinese state buyers purchased up to 650,000 tons of U.S. soybeans, signaling renewed trade after the Trump-Xi summit despite persistent tariff barriers.
Chinese state-owned trading companies purchased eight to 10 cargoes of U.S. soybeans during the week of October 14, 2026, marking the first confirmed transactions since Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping met in Washington in September. The purchases, representing approximately 520,000 to 650,000 metric tons, offer a potentially important signal for American soybean farmers after weeks of limited Chinese buying. The renewed activity matters because China remains a critical destination for U.S. agricultural exports, while unresolved tariffs continue to complicate trade flows and commodity price expectations.
The transactions were reported Wednesday by Reuters journalists Ella Cao and Karl Plume, citing three sources familiar with the grain trade. The cargoes are scheduled for shipment beginning in December, with each Panamax vessel carrying approximately 65,000 metric tons. According to one trader, Chinese buyers paid premiums ranging from $3.10 to $3.20 per bushel above January soybean futures on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT). These premiums reflect the physical export market and should not be confused with an equivalent increase in futures prices or the cash prices received by U.S. producers.
The timing is particularly significant for the American agricultural sector, where producers are closely monitoring export opportunities, input costs and commodity prices. Chinese demand had remained subdued for several weeks, partly because of weaker purchasing activity surrounding the country's National Day holiday earlier in October. The latest orders indicate that state-backed importers are again willing to secure U.S. supplies, although a limited round of purchases does not necessarily establish a sustained recovery in demand. For exporters, grain elevators and agricultural co-ops, the next question is whether additional orders will follow.
Tariff Uncertainty Clouds China's Return to the U.S. Soybean Market
Despite the renewed buying, soybeans remain excluded from the tariff reductions proposed after the September Trump-Xi summit, a major obstacle to a broader recovery in bilateral agricultural trade. The exclusion has discouraged expectations that privately owned Chinese soybean crushers will resume substantial purchases from the United States. State-owned trading companies have therefore played a central role in the latest transactions. This distinction is important because government-directed purchases can support export volumes without necessarily indicating stronger commercial demand from China's processing industry.
Before this week's transactions, China had purchased approximately 13.7 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans, exceeding half of the 25 million-ton purchase target for the 2026/27 marketing year announced by the White House. The additional cargoes could bring cumulative purchases to roughly 14.22 million to 14.35 million tons, assuming the reported volumes are additional to that earlier total. That would leave approximately 10.65 million to 10.78 million tons to reach the target. However, purchase commitments, confirmed export sales and physically shipped volumes are different measures and should not be treated as interchangeable.
Recent Chinese market indicators also suggest that import demand remains uneven. According to data from China's General Administration of Customs cited by Reuters, soybean imports reached 11.88 million metric tons in September, down 7.7% from a year earlier. Meanwhile, state grain reserve company Sinograin sold only 40.5% of the 518,000 metric tons of imported soybeans offered at auction Tuesday, according to agricultural consultancy Mysteel. That represents approximately 210,000 tons sold, suggesting that buyers remain selective even as government authorities continue managing domestic soybean inventories.
The auction results carry implications for U.S. exporters because domestic soybean availability in China can influence the timing and volume of new import orders. Additional reserve auctions are expected in the coming weeks, potentially providing further evidence of demand from feed manufacturers and oilseed processors. The relationship between soybean meal consumption, livestock production and crushing margins will remain important in assessing China's import appetite. For U.S. market participants, stronger government purchasing would be more encouraging if accompanied by consistent private-sector orders and improving demand from China's livestock supply chain.
For American farmers, renewed Chinese buying could help reinforce export expectations during the 2026/27 marketing year, particularly in major soybean-producing states such as Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota and Indiana. However, the effect on farm-level prices will depend on the pace of additional sales, competing global supplies, transportation costs and CBOT futures movements. Basis levels, storage expenses and export logistics will determine how much of any improvement reaches producers. Farmers making marketing decisions must also weigh crop insurance coverage, financing costs and broader uncertainty surrounding U.S. agricultural trade policy.
The developments also have implications for South American exporters, particularly Brazil, which competes directly with the United States for Chinese soybean demand. A sustained shift toward American supplies could alter seasonal trade flows, export premiums and international purchasing patterns. Nevertheless, the current transactions are too limited to demonstrate a structural change in China's sourcing strategy. Global soybean markets will continue responding to production prospects, harvest timing, freight rates and policy decisions affecting the agricultural supply chain. Trade diversification and competitive pricing remain central to China's purchasing strategy.
The latest purchases provide Washington with a tangible agricultural trade development following the September presidential summit, but substantial uncertainty remains. China's willingness to buy additional U.S. soybeans without broader tariff relief will be a critical test of the durability of the renewed trade relationship. For farmers, agribusinesses and commodity investors, attention now turns to subsequent purchase announcements, USDA export sales reporting and Chinese import activity. The central issue is whether these initial cargoes represent the beginning of a sustained commercial recovery or another temporary round of state-directed agricultural purchases.

articles.title: Can Mexico seal a trade deal with Trump before midterms? $872 billion says they'd better. - Latin Times
articles.summary: Can Mexico seal a trade deal with Trump before midterms? $872 billion says they'd better.  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
Mexico and the United States are in a quiet sprint. With the November 3 midterm elections now three weeks away, both governments are pushing to announce a framework agreement on the USMCA's future before American voters head to the polls — though as of Monday, October 12, no deal has been reached.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed at her morning press conference that talks remain active, responding to U.S. President Donald Trump's remarks at a Saturday campaign rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, where he said he intends to close a new trade deal with Mexico. The two sides are not far apart on broad intentions — only on timeline and structure. Mexico and Canada have both sought a 16-year renewal of the agreement, while Washington has proposed a 10-year term paired with annual reviews. On whether the longer option remains available, Sheinbaum told reporters: "That possibility is not closed."
The Review That Reset Everything
The current phase of negotiations was triggered on July 1, 2026, when the USMCA Free Trade Commission held its mandatory six-year joint review. Washington's trade representative formally declined to renew the agreement in its current form, activating the annual review mechanism enshrined in Article 34.7 of the deal. Under that mechanism, the three parties must reassess every year; without a new agreement, the treaty expires July 1, 2036.
Three formal negotiating rounds between Washington and Mexico City were held between May and July 2026, covering automotive rules of origin, steel and aluminum duties, energy provisions, and agricultural market access. In a Senate Finance Committee hearing last July, USTR Jamieson Greer said the administration may have "options for interim arrangements" before the year is out — language that suggests a partial deal rather than a full treaty extension may be on offer.
What Mexico Has — and What Is at Risk
The economic weight behind these negotiations is difficult to overstate. US–Mexico goods trade hit a record $872 billion in 2025 — equivalent to roughly $2.4 billion changing hands every day — and Mexico has been the United States' top goods trading partner for three consecutive years. The Congressional Research Service notes that more than 80 percent of Mexico's exports are shipped to the United States, making the bilateral relationship the structural backbone of the Mexican economy.
Mexico's position within the North American trade architecture is real but conditional. In April 2026, Mexico accounted for 16.9 percent of all U.S. goods imports — a monthly record driven by electronics, auto parts, and advanced manufacturing shipments. Goods that meet USMCA rules of origin enter the United States duty-free; those that do not face tariffs of 25 percent or higher, on top of a 50 percent Section 232 levy on steel and aluminum. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard has made reducing those metal duties, and the 25 percent charge on automobiles, Mexico's clearest demand in every round of talks.
Canada's Absence Changes the Entire Equation
The bilateral dynamic intensified sharply when US–Canada negotiations fell apart in late August. On August 22, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the suspension of trade talks with Washington, saying last-minute U.S. demands had undermined a nearly completed deal. The United States responded with a 50 percent tariff on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods; Ottawa retaliated in kind. USTR Greer said no new talks with Canada were planned.
That rupture cast a long shadow over the USMCA's future as a three-country framework. Sheinbaum has been careful not to be drawn into the US–Canada standoff, consistently declining to suggest Mexico would coordinate with Ottawa or push for a side deal. The calculation is deliberate: maintaining a distinct bilateral channel to Washington is Mexico's most valuable diplomatic card right now.
Rating agency Moody's has flagged the structural risk in this dynamic, warning in August that the T-MEC review could drift primarily toward a bilateral arrangement between Mexico and the U.S. — a process that might not conclude until 2027, sustaining commercial and investment uncertainty across the region.
The Closing Political Window
Both sides understand the calendar is working against them. A trade announcement before November 3 would carry significant electoral weight for Trump's Republican Party, which entered the midterm cycle with narrow majorities in both chambers and now faces unfavorable early polling. Delivering a tangible win in a high-profile foreign economic relationship — one that directly affects manufacturing and agricultural jobs in swing states — would give Republican candidates a concrete argument for voters.
For Sheinbaum, a favorable outcome validates her strategy of patient, disciplined engagement. In a September 18 statement reported by Reuters, she said her government is doing everything possible, "within the framework of sovereignty, respect, and what is best for Mexico, to reach a deal soon." Whether that deal takes shape as a full 16-year renewal, a shorter bridging framework with annual reviews, or a partial sector agreement, what gets signed — or fails to get signed — in the next three weeks will set the commercial rules of North America for the rest of the decade.
